# Functional and numeric graph candidate probes

These small, version-specific research probes record observations behind the
TypeScript graph foundations investigation of 7 September 2026. A passing run
means that the recorded behaviour was reproduced, including identified defects;
it does **not** mean every candidate passed a graph conformance suite.

## Reproduce

From this directory, with Node.js available:

```sh
npm ci --ignore-scripts --no-audit --no-fund
node behaviour-probes.mjs > behaviour-results.json
node type-probes.mjs > type-results.json
node --expose-gc equal-workload.mjs ../oce > equal-workload-results.json
```

The scripts make no network requests, emit JSON to standard output, and exit
nonzero if observations differ. Behaviour/type probes use small finite cases;
the separate lifecycle benchmark uses the pinned corpus. Installation uses exact
top-level versions and the supplied transitive lockfile; lifecycle scripts are
disabled. `effect4` is an npm alias so stable and RC versions coexist.

Original environment: Node 24.19.0, V8 13.6.233.17-node.51, Linux x64;
TypeScript 5.9.3. See the JSON outputs for the executed environment and full
expected/observed values.

## Scope

Behavioural probes cover Effect 3 and 4 ownership/multiplicity; Effect 4 edge
paths, degree, repeated traversal and snapshot allocation history; Rimbu equality,
counts, builders, streams and snapshots; thi.ng loop enumeration/counts, isolated
membership, undirected Floyd-Warshall, inversion and DGraph removal semantics.

The type probes create virtual TypeScript source files in memory. Their full
source is also embedded in the output JSON. `@ts-expect-error` assertions check
that invalid lines really are rejected: an unexpectedly accepted line yields
TypeScript diagnostic 2578. The Effect 4 ES2022-only case deliberately expects
diagnostic 2304 for `Disposable` and `AsyncDisposable`; the subsequent case adds
`ESNext.Disposable` and expects clean compilation with `skipLibCheck:false`.

The behaviour/type probes do not benchmark performance. None of these probes
proves general correctness, tests all algorithms, verifies runtime portability
beyond the recorded environment, or audits vulnerabilities. Source-inspected
complexity claims are separate evidence.

No findings from stable Effect 3 are automatically attributed to Effect 4 RC.
Snapshots preserve active graph identities, not allocator history, as the E4
contract documents. JSON encodes non-finite numeric observations as strings so
`Infinity` is not silently changed to `null`.

## Equal-output lifecycle comparison

`equal-workload.mjs` additionally requires the OCE checkout (default `../oce`) at
commit `dfe92492711f8d7c6ac8233735994c8fada45e0e`, and compares Effect 4 RC,
Graphology 0.26.0 and a source-indexed native snapshot on its generated corpus.
It selects 23 unit roots at unit ordinals 0,80,...,1760 and queries depth two.
Every implementation must return identical BFS node IDs and all member-induced
edge occurrences, with original edge payloads in source ordinal order. An
independent full-edge-list oracle checks complete output equality.

Five rotating-order repetitions measure full build/conversion, first and reused
23-query batches, publication of 100 appended edges, and the updated query batch.
All retain the old snapshot, which is queried again to verify preservation.
Native publication rebuilds the index; Effect clones its structure through
scoped mutation; Graphology copies its graph before updating. Payloads are shared
read-only. Parsing/freezing input and correctness checks are outside timing.
This is a narrow same-output adapter comparison, not a test of ecosystem-wide
algorithm reuse or a basis for deciding long-term ownership by timing alone.
